title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
short: Parallel lines share a slope; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
trouble: Students make a perpendicular slope negative but forget to take the reciprocal, or the reverse.

blocks.html: Slope describes direction, so it can tell you how two lines sit relative to each other. You will use slopes and point-slope form together here.

Parallel lines never meet, so neither can be steeper than the other: they have the same slope (and different intercepts). For perpendicular lines, picture a slope triangle with run $3$ and rise $2$, so slope $\frac{2}{3}$. Turn it a quarter turn: the run becomes $2$ and the rise becomes $-3$, so the new slope is $-\frac{3}{2}$. Turning a quarter turn always swaps rise and run and changes one sign. So perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals, and their product is $-1$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f$ has slope $m$ and $g$ has slope $-\frac{1}{m}$. Move the slider: the lines stay at a right angle.

blocks.html: Parallel: $m_1 = m_2$. Perpendicular: $m_1 \cdot m_2 = -1$, so $m_2 = -\frac{1}{m_1}$ (flip and change the sign).

blocks.title: A parallel line
blocks.q: Write the line through $(3, 1)$ parallel to $y = -2x + 5$.

blocks.title: A perpendicular line
blocks.q: Write the line through $(4, -1)$ perpendicular to $y = \frac{2}{3}x - 1$.
steps: Negative reciprocal of $\frac{2}{3}$: flip it to $\frac{3}{2}$ and change the sign: $-\frac{3}{2}$.

blocks.title: Classify
blocks.q: Are $y = 4x - 1$ and $x + 4y = 8$ parallel, perpendicular, or neither?

blocks.html: Doing only half of “negative reciprocal”: changing the sign but not flipping, or flipping but not changing the sign. The perpendicular slope to $\frac{2}{3}$ is neither $-\frac{2}{3}$ nor $\frac{3}{2}$; it is $-\frac{3}{2}$. Check by multiplying the two slopes: you must get $-1$.
